nodes.name: Unit fraction as one of b equal parts of a whole
nodes.statement: 1/b names the quantity formed by one part when a whole is partitioned into b equal parts.
nodes.assess: This rectangle is split into 6 equal parts and one is shaded. What fraction of the rectangle is shaded?

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement defines 1/b by a whole partitioned into b equal parts, which is exactly partitioning a region into equal shares.

nodes.name: Non-unit fraction as a parts of size 1/b
nodes.statement: a/b names the quantity formed by a parts, each of size 1/b, of a whole partitioned into b equal parts.
nodes.assess: A bar is split into 8 equal parts and 3 are shaded. What fraction of the bar is shaded?

proposed_edges.rationale: The numerator a is the count of selected parts of size 1/b, so reading a/b requires counting the shaded parts.
The statement defines a/b as a parts each of size 1/b, so the unit fraction 1/b is the unit being collected.

nodes.name: Locate a unit fraction on the number line
nodes.statement: 1/b is the point reached by partitioning the interval from 0 to 1 into b equal lengths and taking one of those lengths from 0. Equivalently, 1/b is the length that, laid off b times from 0, reaches 1.
nodes.assess: Place 1/4 on a number line marked only with 0 and 1.
procedure: Mark 0 and 1 on a number line.
Partition the interval from 0 to 1 into b equal lengths.
Label the endpoint of the first length from 0 as 1/b.

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement reuses the meaning of 1/b as one of b equal parts, with the interval from 0 to 1 playing the role of the whole.
The second characterization, 1/b as the length that laid off b times from 0 reaches 1, is unit iteration with 1/b as the unit.
Step 1 marks 0 and 1 on a number line, treating the interval from 0 to 1 as a length on the whole-number line.
Step 2 partitions the interval from 0 to 1 into b equal lengths, which is partitioning a length into equal parts.

nodes.name: Locate a non-unit fraction on the number line
nodes.statement: a/b is the endpoint reached by marking off a lengths of size 1/b from 0 on the number line.
nodes.assess: Place 5/6 on a number line marked only with 0 and 1.
procedure: Mark off a copies of the length 1/b, end to end, starting at 0.
Label the endpoint of the last copy as a/b.

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement reads a/b as a lengths of size 1/b, carrying over the meaning of a/b as a parts each of size 1/b.
Step 1 locates 1/b on the number line, which is exactly the unit-fraction number-line procedure.
Step 2 marks off a copies of the length 1/b end to end from 0, which is laying a unit length end to end.

nodes.name: A fraction is a number
nodes.statement: A fraction names a single point on the number line, so it is a number of the same kind as a whole number, with a definite size and position.
nodes.assess: Is 3/4 more than 0? Less than 1? Mark where it goes between 0 and 2.

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement says a fraction names a single point on the number line, which is the point located by marking off a lengths of 1/b.
The claim that a fraction is a number of the same kind as a whole number relies on whole numbers being points on the same line.

nodes.name: Whole numbers written as fractions
nodes.statement: Any whole number can be written as a fraction: n = n/1, and 1 = b/b for any b, because both name the same point on the number line.
nodes.assess: Write 3 as a fraction. Write 1 as a fraction with denominator 6.

proposed_edges.rationale: The reason given, that n and n/1 name the same point, treats fractions and whole numbers as numbers on one line.
Locating b/b at 1 and n/1 at n requires marking off b lengths of 1/b, or n lengths of 1/1, from 0.
The justification compares the point n/1 with the point of the whole number n, which is n unit lengths from 0.

nodes.name: Equivalent fractions as the same amount of the same whole
nodes.statement: Two fractions are equivalent when they cover the same amount of the same whole.
nodes.assess: These two equal-size bars show 1/2 and 2/4 shaded. Are the fractions equal? How do you know?

proposed_edges.rationale: Covering the same amount of the same whole is judged by direct comparison of the two shaded regions, as in the assessment bars.
The statement compares the amount each fraction covers, which requires reading a/b as a parts of size 1/b of the whole.

nodes.name: Equivalent fractions as the same point on the number line
nodes.statement: Two fractions are equivalent when they name the same point on the number line.
nodes.assess: On this number line, 2/3 and 4/6 are marked. Are they equivalent? How do you know?

proposed_edges.rationale: Two fractions being equivalent means they are the same number, because each names a single point.
The definition requires knowing which point each fraction names, which is the non-unit fraction number-line location.

nodes.name: Recognize and generate simple equivalent fractions with a model
nodes.statement: Using a fraction model with denominators 2, 3, 4, 6, or 8, find a fraction that covers the same amount as a given one by splitting or joining its parts.
nodes.assess: Use a fraction strip to find a fraction equal to 2/3 with denominator 6.
procedure: Show the given fraction on a model.
Split each part into equal smaller parts, or join equal groups of parts.
Count the new number of shaded parts and total parts and write the new fraction.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 3 counts the new number of shaded parts and the new total number of parts to get the numerator and denominator.
The statement asks for a fraction that covers the same amount as the given one, which is the same-size meaning of equivalence.
Step 1 shows the given fraction on a model and step 3 writes the new fraction, both using a/b as a shaded of b equal parts.
Step 2 splits each part into equal smaller parts, which is partitioning a region of the strip or area model into equal shares.

nodes.name: Explain why simple equivalent fractions are equal
nodes.statement: For a specific pair such as 1/2 and 2/4, a model shows the two fractions cover the same amount of the same whole, so they are equal.
nodes.assess: Explain, with a drawing, why 1/2 = 2/4.

proposed_edges.rationale: The explanation concludes equality because the two fractions cover the same amount of the same whole, which is the same-size criterion.
The model in the explanation draws each fraction, such as 2/4, as a shaded parts of a whole cut into b equal parts.
The assessment asks for a drawing, so the learner must partition two same-size wholes into halves and fourths themselves.

nodes.name: Compare fractions with the same denominator
nodes.statement: When two fractions have the same denominator, the parts are the same size, so the fraction with more parts is greater.
nodes.assess: Which is greater, 3/8 or 5/8? Explain.

proposed_edges.rationale: Deciding that the fraction with more parts is greater means comparing the two numerators as whole numbers.
On the number line a/b is a copies of the same length 1/b from 0, so more copies reach a point farther right.
The reason that the parts are the same size uses a/b as a parts each of size 1/b, with b shared by both fractions.

nodes.name: Compare fractions with the same numerator
nodes.statement: When two fractions have the same numerator, there are the same number of parts, so the fraction whose parts are larger (smaller denominator) is greater.
nodes.assess: Which is greater, 2/3 or 2/5? Explain.

proposed_edges.rationale: Identifying which fraction has the smaller denominator requires comparing the two denominators as whole numbers.
The argument that both fractions have the same number of parts reads each fraction as a parts of size 1/b.
The statement compares part sizes 1/3 and 1/5, each defined as one of b equal parts of the whole.
The statement uses that the fraction with the smaller denominator has larger parts, which is comparing unit fractions 1/b of the same whole.
The conclusion that the smaller denominator gives larger parts uses the fact that more equal parts of a whole means smaller parts.
The step that a smaller denominator gives larger parts uses the fact that more equal shares of one whole are smaller shares (1.G.A.3).
The reason a smaller denominator means larger parts is that cutting the same whole into more equal shares makes each share smaller.

nodes.name: Compare fractions by reasoning about their size
nodes.statement: Decide which of two fractions is greater by reasoning about the size of the parts and how many there are.
nodes.assess: Which is greater, 3/4 or 3/6? Which is greater, 2/6 or 5/6?

proposed_edges.rationale: Reasoning about how many parts there are, as in 2/6 versus 5/6, is the same-denominator comparison.
Reasoning about the size of the parts, as in 3/4 versus 3/6, is the same-numerator comparison.

nodes.name: Fraction comparisons need the same whole
nodes.statement: Comparing two fractions by size is only valid when both refer to the same whole; 1/2 of a small pizza can be less than 1/3 of a large one.
nodes.assess: Sam says 1/2 is always bigger than 1/3. When could 1/3 of something be bigger than 1/2 of something?

proposed_edges.rationale: Seeing that 1/2 of a small pizza can be less than 1/3 of a large one means comparing the actual pieces directly.
The statement qualifies when a comparison of two fractions by size is valid, so comparing by size must already be known.
The claim being qualified, that 1/2 is bigger than 1/3, is a same-numerator comparison that holds only for one whole.
The claim depends on 1/b being defined as a part of a particular whole, so its amount changes with the whole.
The pizza example only has force against the fact that 1/2 is greater than 1/3 when both are taken of the same whole.

nodes.name: Record fraction comparisons with >, =, <
nodes.statement: The result of comparing two fractions is written with the symbols >, =, or <.
nodes.assess: Write >, =, or < between 4/6 and 2/6.

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement records comparisons with the symbols >, =, < whose meaning was set for whole number comparisons.
Writing 4/6 > 2/6 asserts an order between two numbers, which requires treating each fraction as a number with a definite size.
The statement records the result of comparing two fractions, so a fraction comparison must first be made.
The assessment pair 4/6 and 2/6 must first be compared by the same-denominator reasoning before a symbol is written.

nodes.name: Justify a fraction comparison
nodes.statement: A comparison of fractions with the same numerator or the same denominator is justified by a model or an argument about part size and number of parts.
nodes.assess: Use a drawing to show why 2/3 > 2/5.

proposed_edges.rationale: Justifying a same-denominator comparison uses the argument that more parts of the same size give more.
Justifying a same-numerator comparison such as 2/3 > 2/5 uses the argument that equal counts of larger parts give more.
A justifying model is valid only if both fractions are drawn on wholes of the same size, which is the same-whole condition.
The model in the justification draws each fraction as a shaded parts of a whole partitioned into b equal parts.
The assessment drawing requires partitioning two same-size wholes into thirds and fifths to show 2/3 > 2/5.

nodes.name: Compare fractions in a story about shares
nodes.statement: A story problem gives two fractional shares of same-size wholes; the learner decides which share is larger and explains why.
nodes.assess: Ana ate 2/6 of a pizza and Ben ate 2/8 of a pizza the same size. Who ate more? Explain.

proposed_edges.rationale: The learner must explain why one share is larger, which is justifying the comparison by part size and number of parts.
Deciding which fractional share in the story is larger uses reasoning about part size and number of parts.
The test problem compares 2/6 and 2/8, which share a numerator, so the same-numerator rule settles it.
The story's stipulation of same-size wholes, such as pizzas of the same size, is what makes the comparison of shares valid.
The learner translates '2/6 of a pizza' in the story into 2 of 6 equal slices of a whole pizza.

nodes.name: Generate equivalent fractions with a/b = (n x a)/(n x b)
nodes.statement: For any whole number n greater than 0, a/b = (n x a)/(n x b), so multiplying numerator and denominator by n gives an equivalent fraction.
nodes.assess: Write two fractions equivalent to 3/5.
procedure: Choose a whole number n greater than 0.
Multiply the numerator by n and the denominator by n.
Write the result as the equivalent fraction.

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement claims the result is an equivalent fraction, which means it names the same point on the number line as a/b.
The rule a/b = (n x a)/(n x b) asserts equivalence, meaning the same amount of the same whole.
The rule generalizes the model pattern in which splitting each part into n pieces multiplies shaded and total parts by n.
Step 2 multiplies the numerator by n and the denominator by n, which uses single-digit multiplication facts.

nodes.name: Recognize equivalent fractions with a/b = (n x a)/(n x b)
nodes.statement: Decide whether two fractions are equivalent by checking whether one is obtained from the other by multiplying numerator and denominator by the same whole number.
nodes.assess: Is 4/10 equivalent to 2/5? Is 6/8 equivalent to 3/5?
procedure: Find whether the larger denominator is a whole-number multiple n of the smaller one.
Check whether the corresponding numerator is the same multiple n.
Conclude equivalent if both use the same n.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 1 asks whether the larger denominator is a whole-number multiple of the smaller, which is how many groups of the smaller fit.
Recognition checks whether one fraction is obtained from the other by multiplying numerator and denominator by the same n, the generate rule.
Concluding that two fractions are not equivalent, as for 6/8 and 3/5, rests on the meaning of equivalence as same amount.
Step 1 decides whether the larger denominator is a multiple n of the smaller, and step 2 checks the numerators, both by multiplication facts.

nodes.name: Explain why a/b = (n x a)/(n x b)
nodes.statement: Splitting each of the b parts into n equal parts multiplies the number of parts by n and the number of chosen parts by n, while the amount covered does not change; so (n x a)/(n x b) is the same amount as a/b, for every n.
nodes.assess: Use a visual fraction model to explain why 2/3 = (4 x 2)/(4 x 3), and say why the same argument works for any n.

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement explains the identity a/b = (n x a)/(n x b), so the learner must know the rule being justified.
The conclusion that the amount covered does not change, so the fractions are equal, uses the same-amount meaning of equivalence.
The general argument for every n extends the specific-pair model explanation, such as 1/2 = 2/4, to an arbitrary splitting factor.
The argument splits each of the b parts into n equal parts, which is the split step of the model procedure done for a general n.
The argument models a/b as a chosen parts out of b equal parts of a whole before splitting them.
Counting the new parts as b groups of n, and the chosen parts as a groups of n, gives n x b and n x a by equal groups.
The argument splits each of the b parts into n equal smaller parts, an equal-share partition of each part.
